claims.text: In single-phase high-entropy alloys, hardness and strength are primarily governed by lattice distortion.
Atomic size mismatches produce local lattice strain and distortion.
Local lattice distortions caused by atomic size mismatch elevate the energy barriers for dislocation motion.
Elevated barriers to dislocation motion enhance hardness.
Elevated barriers to dislocation motion increase resistance to plastic deformation.
Alloys with greater atomic size mismatch will have greater lattice distortion than alloys with minimal mismatch.
Alloys with greater atomic size mismatch will exhibit higher hardness than the minimal-mismatch baseline.
Alloys with greater atomic size mismatch will exhibit higher tensile strength than the minimal-mismatch baseline.
A minimal-atomic-size-mismatch high-entropy alloy will have relatively low lattice distortion.
Lower lattice distortion in the baseline will result in lower hardness and tensile strength.
X-ray diffraction peak broadening can be used to quantify the relevant local lattice strain or distortion.
Transmission electron microscopy strain mapping can quantify the relevant local lattice strain or distortion.
The proposed size-mismatch mechanism is expected to govern behavior in single-phase, disordered solid-solution high-entropy alloys whose deformation is dominated by dislocation motion.
The proposed relationship may not apply when precipitation, ordering, diffusion, or creep substantially contributes to deformation.

contradictions.description: The intervention says alloy composition will be systematically varied to change atomic size mismatch, whereas the falsification design calls for alloys that are identical in overall composition except for atomic size mismatch. Because atomic size mismatch is determined by elemental identities and fractions, the stated design cannot generally vary it while retaining an identical overall composition.
